source.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
source.authors: Shashank Sule; Xinyue Yu; Boonam Shin; Yuxuan Liu; Abolfazl Hashemi; Hayden Schaeffer

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests curvature and memorization in diffusion models, extending the study to a generative-model setting. It does not test the claim versions' supervised classification outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study measures generated-copy frequency, input curvature, and counterfactual loss in diffusion models. These are findings about memorization, but they do not measure the supervised test-error outcomes or weight-perturbation sharpness specified by V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study measures generated copying, input-loss curvature, and counterfactual denoising-loss differences in diffusion models. None measures V1–V8. In particular, input curvature is not V7's magnitude-scaled weight sharpness, and removing examples to measure copying does not test V8's classification-accuracy penalty relative to random removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors find aggregate input curvature useful for tracking generated copying, while individual-image curvature fails to predict copy count. They derive an assumption-dependent bound involving leave-one-out input curvature and nearest-neighbor distance, and assess loss differences using leave-10-out experiments. They explicitly leave unresolved whether curvature dominates the ELBO gap, so the theory does not establish an unconditional predictor of sampling likelihood. They also acknowledge late-training breakdown and limitations of the proposed stopping statistic.
record.recipe_differences: Studies diffusion-model memorization and curvature proxies, not supervised classification generalization or the interventions and measures specified in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and training-set size change the timing and amount of memorization; DDPM sample-prediction ImageNet n=10240 is reported to remain generalizing by the k=1/3 criterion while its curvature barely changes. The counterfactual curvature relation breaks down in the highly overfitted tail.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregate training input curvature rises with generated copying; validation curvature separates from training curvature and can exhibit a local minimum. The proposed relative-curvature maximum can occur after substantial memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregate input-curvature trends can indicate generated-copy memorization during training in the tested diffusion models.

fits_no_version.finding: Copied ImageNet images generally have higher input-Hessian trace, but individual-image curvature does not predict copy frequency in the CelebA experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group-level curvature differences need not provide individual-sample copy-frequency prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: The explicitly described ImageNet n=1024 DDPM experiment has lower final copying and lower training input curvature after removing the ten most copied examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing highly copied training examples can reduce generated copying in diffusion models.

fits_no_version.finding: Leave-10-out input curvature roughly corresponds to counterfactual denoising-loss dynamics, with correspondence breaking down late in highly overfitted training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out input curvature may proxy counterfactual loss influence during some phases of diffusion-model training.

record.problems: The authors describe evidence from only ImageNet and CelebA and say the bound depends on assumptions; whether curvature dominates the ELBO gap is unsettled. The relative train–validation curvature maximum can occur after memorization is already high. Several results are trends shown in figures without transcribed numeric values, and the counterfactual empirical estimate uses a leave-10-out model as a proxy for leave-one-out retraining.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from Appendix D's figures 21–29 and 31–33 or Appendix E's Figures 38 and 27–29: these contain related curvature and memorization trends, but the reported results are substantially covered by R1–R6 or do not add a distinct outcome for a claim version. Figure-only details without descriptive outcomes were not transcribed as numerical values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label versus random-label accuracy using the same architecture and training recipe.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifier test error and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects on classifier test error across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with train–test error gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Classification test-accuracy loss after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because every row measures a different construct; this does not negate the study's own reported effects. The study is not an original source for these versions, but no version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy in the specified classifiers.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects on classifier test error.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation sharpness and supervised train–test gaps.
Classification test accuracy after removing memorized examples from ResNet-50.

rows.subject: DDPMs on CelebA, n=128 and n=10240
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base channel width W=64; training set sizes n=128 and n=10240
rows.operation_detail: Tracked mean training input curvature and generated-sample memorization fraction over training time.
rows.measure: Mean training curvature rises over training together with fmem; n=128 memorizes earlier, while for n=10240 memorization is delayed until τ ≈ 105.
rows.value: Curvature rises with fmem; the paper says training curvature is already increasing while fmem is still flat.
rows.locator: Section 3, Figure 1 panels C and D; Appendix D, Figures 21–22
rows.note: The text reports trends, not numerical curvature values.
rows.check: The reported curvature and copying trends bear on no version. The delayed onset is approximately 10^5 training steps.

rows.subject: DDPMs on CelebA, n=128 and n=10240
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base channel width W=64; training set sizes n=128 and n=10240
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean training and validation input curvature over training time against fmem.
rows.measure: Validation curvature separates from training curvature when fmem starts accelerating; for n=10240 memorization is delayed until τ ≈ 105.
rows.baseline: Training and validation curvature track together before separation.
rows.value: They diverge at the step where fmem starts to accelerate.
rows.locator: Section 3, Figure 1 panels A, B, and D; Appendix D, Figure 26
rows.note: A stopping criterion is proposed from the relative curvature difference; the paper says the local maximum can indicate a period of already high memorization.
rows.check: Train–validation input-curvature separation does not measure any version. Figure 26 concerns flow matching on CelebA n=128, not the row's DDPM conditions.

rows.subject: DDPMs on ImageNet-1K, training set sizes n=128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096
rows.operation_detail: Tracked mean training and validation input curvature and generated-sample memorization fraction.
rows.measure: Training curvature rises; validation curvature reaches a local minimum and then rises as memorization proceeds. fmem reaches 100% by τ ≈ 106 for every model except n=4096.
rows.baseline: Validation loss falls throughout training for every n.
rows.value: Validation curvature's local minimum and subsequent rise accompany heavy memorization; n=4096 is the stated exception to fmem reaching 100%.
rows.locator: Section 3, Figure 2 panels A, E, and F; Appendix E
rows.note: The paper reports trends and an exception; most plotted values are not transcribed numerically.
rows.check: No version applies. The source is internally inconsistent: Section 3 says all sizes except 4096 reach 100% copying, but Appendix C reports peaks of 85.0%, 19.9%, and 0.57% for n=512, 1024, and 2048, respectively. Do not present the Section 3 assertion as settled. Appendix E measures input-Hessian trace, rather than the squared Frobenius norm defined in the main text.

rows.subject: DDPMs on ImageNet-1K, training set sizes n=128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096
rows.operation_detail: Compared curvature of copied and non-copied training images at evaluated checkpoints.

conditions.value: F(i, τ) > 0 versus F(i, τ) = 0; group plotted only with at least ten images

rows.measure: Copied images generally have higher mean curvature than the remaining training images; separation varies with training size and checkpoint.
rows.baseline: Remaining training images at the same checkpoint.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error across images in each group, shown as shading.
rows.note: The stated relationship varies in separation; numerical group means are figure-only.
rows.check: The copied-versus-non-copied comparison bears on no version. Specify input-Hessian trace, as Figure 37 does. Groups are defined separately at each checkpoint; the comparison group need not consist of images never copied during training.

rows.subject: DDPMs on CelebA, n=128 and n=10240
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base channel width W=64; training set sizes n=128 and n=10240
rows.operation_detail: Compared each training image's curvature with its generated copy count.
rows.measure: Once memorization is heavy, every training image is reproduced at different frequencies, but individual-image curvature does not predict copy count.
rows.value: Individual curvature does not predict copy count.
rows.note: This is an explicit negative result for sample-level copy-count prediction.
rows.check: The explicit failure of individual-image curvature to predict copy count is a result about a different construct, not absence of any V1–V8 effect.

rows.subject: ImageNet DDPM noise-prediction models, full training set versus leave-10-out
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base width 64; n=128 and n=1024, with top 10 memorized examples removed for leave-10-out models
rows.stage_stated: during training and at end of training
rows.operation_detail: Retrained after removing the top 10 memorized training samples; compared generated-copy fraction and mean training curvature.
rows.measure: Leave-10-out model has lower memorization score at end of training and lower input loss curvature for all training steps.
rows.value: Lower memorization score at end of training and lower curvature throughout training.
rows.locator: Appendix D, Figure 30 and text describing Figure 30; Figures 32–33 for n=128
rows.note: The paper says removal improves generalization, but reports generated-copy fraction rather than classification test accuracy.
rows.check: Reduced copying and input curvature do not establish V8's test-accuracy effect; there is also no matched random-removal control. The prose explicitly describes the result for n=1024; n=128 is presented as a repeated experiment in figure-only material.

rows.subject: ImageNet DDPM noise-prediction models, n=128 and n=1024, leave-10-out
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base width 64; 10 top memorized examples removed
rows.operation_detail: Tracked per-sample full-model versus leave-10-out loss difference and leave-one-out-model curvature for selected removed samples.
rows.measure: Curvature roughly corresponds to the drops and stability of the counterfactual loss difference; at the very tail, curvature rises while the loss difference keeps falling, and the relation breaks down in the highly overfitted regime.
rows.value: Approximate correspondence through training, with breakdown at the highly overfitted tail.
rows.note: The reported counterfactual is a loss difference using the leave-10-out model as an estimator, not a full leave-one-out retraining per example.
rows.check: The counterfactual loss comparison bears on no version. Correct operation_detail: empirical curvature comes from a leave-10-out model, not a leave-one-out model. Direct sampling log-likelihood differences are not measured.

rows.subject: ImageNet flow-matching models, n=128 and n=1024, leave-10-out
rows.size_stated: U-Net, base width W=64; 10 top memorized examples removed
rows.operation_detail: Tracked per-sample full-model versus leave-10-out loss difference and leave-10-out-model curvature.
rows.measure: The paper shows loss differences and per-sample curvature for the ten removed examples.
rows.value: Figure-only curves; the text does not state a specific outcome for these flow-matching comparisons.
rows.note: No descriptive text gives a result for these plotted curves.
rows.check: This records that curves were plotted without an interpretable outcome in the supplied text. It should not be retained as a result row or used as evidence of correspondence between curvature and loss differences.
